Prevention: The migratory behaviour of armyworm enables them to move each generation to new areas where there are suitable conditions for breeding.
Certain practices make a crop less suitable:
Cut grassy weeds from bordering fields.
Remove weeds regularly to reduce breeding sites and shelter for armyworm
Remove all plant debris after harvesting
Plough and harrow field thoroughly to expose pupae to natural enemies and desiccation
Plough a deep trench around field and fill with water
Monitoring: At the onset of the rainy season regularly monitor for the presence of armyworm:
Programme’s outbreak forecasts. (Listen to radio announcements)
Pheromone traps to determine the main flight period for moths
Look for masses of dark larvae migrating between fields
Look for the presence of larvae or signs of damage to the crop.
Detect larvae by looking under leaves and in leaf whorls (where they feed at night) and under debris and at the base of plants (where they hide during the day)
Report any infestation detected to the
Consider taking action when eggs are present on 5% of seedling or when 25% of plants show signs of feeding damage
Direct Control: For small farms crush egg masses and hand-pick larvae.
Do not use larvae as food, because they are poisonous
Seed extract: 50g/liter water with a little soap; Seed powder mix 1:1-1:2 with sawdust/soil into leaf sheaths; Neem leaves: 50-150g- 1-2 handful/ litre water, soap
Trichogramma wasps that will hatch and then parasitise and kill armyworm eggs (read and follow label instructions)
S. exempta nucleopolyhedrovirus (SpexNPV) against larvae (read and follow label instructions)
Restrictions: When using a pesticide, always wear protective clothing and follow the instructions on the product label, such as dosage, timing of application, pre- harvest interval, max number of sprays, restricted re- entry interval, min retreatment interval.
